## Proposition 1.1
**Statement:** On a given finite straight line to construct an equilateral triangle.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given finite straight line. We are required to construct an equilateral triangle on AB.

**Step 2.** With centre A and distance AB, describe the circle BCD. [P3]

**Step 3.** With centre B and distance BA, describe the circle ACE. [P3]

**Step 4.** Let C be a point in which the circles BCD and ACE intersect one another. From the point C draw the straight line CA to the point A, and the straight line CB to the point B. [P1]

**Step 5.** Since A is the centre of the circle BCD, the straight line AC is equal to the straight line AB. [D1.15]

**Step 6.** Since B is the centre of the circle ACE, the straight line BC is equal to the straight line BA. [D1.15]

**Step 7.** From Steps 5 and 6, both CA and CB are equal to AB. But things which are equal to the same thing are also equal to one another, so CA is equal to CB. [CN1]

**Step 8.** Therefore the three straight lines CA, AB, and BC are equal to one another.

**Step 9.** Since the triangle ABC has all three sides equal, it is equilateral. [D1.20]

**Step 10.** Therefore the equilateral triangle ABC has been constructed on the given finite straight line AB, which is what was required to do.

## Proposition 1.2
**Statement:** To place at a given point (as an extremity) a straight line equal to a given straight line.

**Step 1.** Let A be the given point, and BC the given straight line. It is required to place at point A, as an extremity, a straight line equal to BC.

**Step 2.** Join the point A to the point B by the straight line AB. [P1]

**Step 3.** On the straight line AB, construct an equilateral triangle DAB. [1.1]

**Step 4.** With centre B and distance BC, describe the circle CGH. [P3]

**Step 5.** Produce the straight line DB in a straight line to the point G, where it meets the circle CGH. [P2]

**Step 6.** With centre D and distance DG, describe the circle GKL. [P3]

**Step 7.** Produce the straight line DA in a straight line to the point L, where it meets the circle GKL. [P2]

**Step 8.** Since B is the centre of circle CGH, the straight line BC equals the straight line BG. [D1.15]

**Step 9.** Since D is the centre of circle GKL, the straight line DL equals the straight line DG. [D1.15]

**Step 10.** Since the triangle DAB is equilateral, the straight line DA equals the straight line DB. [D1.20]

**Step 11.** Since DA equals DB (Step 10), and DL equals DG (Step 9), and DA is a part of DL while DB is a part of DG, the remainder AL equals the remainder BG. [CN3]

**Step 12.** Since BC equals BG (Step 8), and AL equals BG (Step 11), the straight line AL equals the straight line BC. [CN1]

**Step 13.** Therefore at the given point A, the straight line AL has been placed as an extremity, equal to the given straight line BC. Which was to be done.

## Proposition 1.3
**Statement:** Given two unequal straight lines, to cut off from the greater a straight line equal to the less.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the greater straight line and C the lesser. It is required to cut off from AB a straight line equal to C.

**Step 2.** At the point A, place a straight line AD equal to C [1.2].

**Step 3.** With centre A and distance AD, describe the circle DEF [P3].

**Step 4.** Since A is the centre of circle DEF, AE is equal to AD [D1.15].

**Step 5.** But AD is equal to C [Step 2]. Therefore AE is also equal to C [CN1].

**Step 6.** Therefore, given two unequal straight lines AB and C, from the greater AB a straight line AE has been cut off equal to the lesser C. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.4
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, they will also have the base equal to the base, the triangle will be equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles will be equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and the angle BAC equal to the angle EDF. We are to prove that the base BC is equal to the base EF, the triangle ABC is equal to the triangle DEF, and the remaining angles are equal respectively, namely angle ABC equals angle DEF, and angle ACB equals angle DFE.

**Step 2.** Apply triangle ABC to triangle DEF so that the point A is placed on the point D, and the straight line AB is placed along the straight line DE. Then, since AB is equal to DE, the point B will coincide with the point E. [CN4]

**Step 3.** Since AB coincides with DE, and the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF, the straight line AC will also coincide in direction with the straight line DF. [Since equal angles placed upon one another coincide.]

**Step 4.** Since AC is equal to DF, and AC has been placed along DF, the point C will coincide with the point F. [CN4]

**Step 5.** But B has already been shown to coincide with E (Step 2). Therefore the base BC will coincide with the base EF. For if, when B coincides with E and C with F, the base BC does not coincide with the base EF, then two different straight lines would enclose a space, which is impossible. [P1] Therefore BC coincides with EF and is equal to it. [CN4]

**Step 6.** Since the base BC coincides with the base EF, the whole triangle ABC coincides with the whole triangle DEF and is equal to it. [CN4]

**Step 7.** And the remaining angles also coincide with the remaining angles respectively and are equal to them: angle ABC equals angle DEF, and angle ACB equals angle DFE. [CN4]

**Step 8.** Therefore, if two triangles have two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have the angles contained by the equal straight lines equal, then the base is equal to the base, the triangle is equal to the triangle, and the remaining angles are equal to the remaining angles respectively, namely those which the equal sides subtend. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.5
**Statement:** In isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and, if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be an isosceles triangle with AB equal to AC. Produce AB to D and AC to E by Postulate P2.

**Step 2.** Take an arbitrary point F on BD. Using Proposition 1.3, cut off from AE a segment AG equal to AF, so that AF equals AG.

**Step 3.** Join FC and GB by Postulate P1.

**Step 4.** Since AF equals AG (by construction in Step 2), and AB equals AC (given), and the angle FAC is common to triangles AFC and AGB, therefore by Proposition 1.4 (SAS), triangle AFC is equal to triangle AGB, and the base FC equals the base GB, and angle ACF equals angle ABG, and angle AFC equals angle AGB.

**Step 5.** Since AF equals AG, and AB equals AC, and AF is greater than AB (since F is on BD beyond B, by Common Notion CN5), subtracting equals from equals by Common Notion CN3, the remainder BF equals the remainder CG.

**Step 6.** In Step 4 it was shown that FC equals GB and BF equals CG (Step 5). Also, angle BFC equals angle CGB, since these are the angles AFC and AGB proved equal in Step 4 (the angle at F in triangle BFC is the same as angle AFC, and the angle at G in triangle CGB is the same as angle AGB). Therefore by Proposition 1.4 (SAS), triangle BFC is equal to triangle CGB, and angle FBC equals angle GCB, and angle BCF equals angle CBG.

**Step 7.** Since the whole angle ABG was proved equal to the whole angle ACF (Step 4), and within these angle CBG equals angle BCF (Step 6), subtracting equals from equals by Common Notion CN3, the remaining angle ABC equals the remaining angle ACB. These are the angles at the base of the isosceles triangle, which are therefore equal to one another.

**Step 8.** Furthermore, angle FBC was proved equal to angle GCB (Step 6). These are the angles under the base, which are therefore equal to one another.

**Step 9.** Therefore, in isosceles triangles the angles at the base are equal to one another, and if the equal straight lines be produced further, the angles under the base will be equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.6
**Statement:** If in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle having the angle ABC equal to the angle ACB. I say that the side AB is also equal to the side AC.

**Step 2.** For suppose AB is not equal to AC. Then one of them is greater. Let AB be the greater.

**Step 3.** From AB the greater, cut off DB equal to AC the less [1.3].

**Step 4.** Join DC [P1].

**Step 5.** Now in the triangles DBC and ACB, we have DB equal to AC (by construction), BC is common to both triangles, and the angle DBC is equal to the angle ACB (since angle DBC is the same as angle ABC, which is equal to angle ACB by hypothesis). Therefore, by the side-angle-side congruence [1.4], the triangle DBC is equal to the triangle ACB.

**Step 6.** But the triangle DBC is a part of the triangle ACB, since D lies on AB between A and B, so that triangle DBC is contained within triangle ACB. Therefore the part would be equal to the whole, which is impossible [CN5].

**Step 7.** Therefore AB is not unequal to AC; hence AB equals AC.

**Step 8.** Therefore, if in a triangle two angles be equal to one another, the sides which subtend the equal angles will also be equal to one another. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.7
**Statement:** Given two straight lines constructed on a straight line (from its extremities) and meeting in a point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line (from its extremities), and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it.

**Step 1.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that on the straight line AB, from its endpoints A and B, the straight lines AC and BC are constructed meeting at C, and also the straight lines AD and BD are constructed meeting at a different point D on the same side of AB, with AC equal to AD and BC equal to BD. We shall show this leads to an impossibility.

**Step 2.** Join C to D by a straight line [P1].

**Step 3.** Consider first the case where D does not fall within the triangle ACB. Since AC equals AD, the triangle ACD is isosceles with base CD. Produce AC beyond C to a point F, and produce AD beyond D to a point G [P2].

**Step 4.** Since AC equals AD, triangle ACD is isosceles. By Proposition 1.5, the angles under the base are equal: angle FCD equals angle GDC.

**Step 5.** Now, since D does not fall within triangle ACB, the ray CB falls between rays CF and CD at vertex C, so that angle BCD is a part of angle FCD. Therefore, by Common Notion 5, angle FCD is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 6.** Since angle FCD equals angle GDC (Step 4) and angle FCD is greater than angle BCD (Step 5), it follows that angle GDC is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 7.** At vertex D, the ray DB falls between rays DG and DC, so that angle GDC is a part of angle BDC. Therefore, by Common Notion 5, angle BDC is greater than angle GDC.

**Step 8.** Since angle BDC is greater than angle GDC (Step 7) and angle GDC is greater than angle BCD (Step 6), it follows that angle BDC is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 9.** But BC equals BD, so triangle BCD is isosceles with base CD. By Proposition 1.5, angle BCD equals angle BDC.

**Step 10.** Step 8 states that angle BDC is greater than angle BCD, while Step 9 states they are equal. This is a contradiction.

**Step 11.** Now consider the case where D falls within triangle ACB. Join CD as before [P1]. Since AC equals AD, triangle ACD is isosceles with base CD. By Proposition 1.5, angle ACD equals angle ADC.

**Step 12.** Since D falls within triangle ACB, the angle BCD is a part of the angle ACD. Therefore, by Common Notion 5, angle ACD is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 13.** Since angle ACD equals angle ADC (Step 11), it follows that angle ADC is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 14.** Furthermore, since D lies within triangle ACB, at vertex D the ray DC lies between rays DA and DB, so that angle ADC is a part of angle BDC. Therefore, by Common Notion 5, angle BDC is greater than angle ADC. Since angle ADC is already greater than angle BCD (Step 13), it follows a fortiori that angle BDC is greater than angle BCD.

**Step 15.** But BC equals BD, so triangle BCD is isosceles. By Proposition 1.5, angle BCD equals angle BDC.

**Step 16.** Step 14 states that angle BDC is greater than angle BCD, while Step 15 states they are equal. This is a contradiction.

**Step 17.** In both cases, the assumption that two distinct pairs of lines from the endpoints of AB, on the same side, can meet at two different points while being respectively equal leads to a contradiction. Therefore, such a configuration is impossible, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.8
**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DEF be two triangles having the two sides AB, AC equal to the two sides DE, DF respectively, namely AB equal to DE and AC equal to DF, and let the base BC be equal to the base EF. I say that the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 2.** Let the triangle ABC be applied to the triangle DEF, placing the point B on the point E and the straight line BC along the straight line EF. Then, since BC is equal to EF, the point C will coincide with the point F.

**Step 3.** Now BC coinciding with EF, the sides BA and AC must also coincide with the sides ED and DF respectively. For if the base BC coincides with the base EF but the sides BA and CA do not coincide with the sides ED and FD, but take a different position as EG and FG, then on the same straight line EF, from its extremities E and F, and on the same side of it, there will have been constructed two straight lines meeting at G and two other straight lines meeting at D, equal to the former two respectively, namely each to that which has the same extremity with it (since AB equals DE, and so EG equals ED; and since AC equals DF, and so FG equals FD). But this is impossible by Proposition 1.7: given two straight lines constructed on a straight line from its extremities and meeting in a point, there cannot be constructed on the same straight line, from its extremities, and on the same side of it, two other straight lines meeting in another point and equal to the former two respectively.

**Step 4.** Therefore the sides BA and AC do coincide with ED and DF respectively. Thus the angle BAC coincides with the angle EDF, and therefore by Common Notion 4, the angle BAC is equal to the angle EDF.

**Step 5.** Therefore, if two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, and have also the base equal to the base, they will also have the angles equal which are contained by the equal straight lines. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.11
**Statement:** To draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line and C the given point on it. It is required to draw a straight line from C at right angles to AB.

**Step 2.** Take an arbitrary point D on AC. Using Proposition 1.3, cut off CE from CB such that CE equals CD.

**Step 3.** On the segment DE, construct an equilateral triangle DEF by Proposition 1.1.

**Step 4.** Join FC by Postulate 1.

**Step 5.** I claim that the straight line FC has been drawn at right angles to AB from the point C.

**Step 6.** Since DC equals CE (by construction in Step 2), and DF equals EF (since triangle DEF is equilateral, by 1.1), and the side CF is common to triangles DCF and ECF, the two triangles DCF and ECF have three sides equal to three sides respectively. Therefore, by Proposition 1.8 (SSS), the angle DCF equals the angle ECF.

**Step 7.** But the angles DCF and ECF are adjacent angles formed by the straight line FC standing on the straight line DE (which lies along AB). Since these adjacent angles are equal to one another, each of them is a right angle by Definition 1.10, and the straight line FC is perpendicular to AB.

**Step 8.** Therefore the straight line FC has been drawn at right angles to the given straight line AB from the given point C on it, which is what was required to do. [Q.E.F.]

## Proposition 1.12
**Statement:** To a given infinite straight line, from a given point which is not on it, to draw a perpendicular straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given infinite straight line, and let C be the given point which is not on it. It is required to draw a perpendicular straight line from C to AB.

**Step 2.** Take any point D on the other side of line AB from C. With center C and distance CD, describe circle EGD [P3]. This circle, having its center C off the line AB and radius CD reaching to the other side, must cross line AB at two points. Let it meet AB at the points G and E.

**Step 3.** Bisect the straight line GE at the point H [1.10].

**Step 4.** Join CG, CH, and CE [P1].

**Step 5.** Since G and E are both on the circle with center C and distance CD, we have CG = CE [D1.15].

**Step 6.** Since GE was bisected at H, we have GH = HE [1.10]. The side CH is common to triangles CGH and CEH.

**Step 7.** In triangles CGH and CEH, we have CG = CE [Step 5], GH = HE [Step 6], and CH is common. Therefore, by the equality of two sides and the base respectively, the angle CHG equals the angle CHE [1.8].

**Step 8.** But angles CHG and CHE are adjacent angles formed by the straight line CH standing on the straight line GE. Since these adjacent angles are equal to one another, each of them is a right angle, and the straight line CH is perpendicular to GE [D1.10].

**Step 9.** Therefore, from the given point C, which is not on the given infinite straight line AB, the perpendicular CH has been drawn to AB. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.13
**Statement:** If a straight line set up on a straight line make angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line AB be set up on the straight line CD, making angles ABC and ABD. I say that the angles ABC and ABD are either two right angles or equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** If angle ABC is equal to angle ABD, then each of them is a right angle by definition [D1.10]. In this case, the angles ABC and ABD are two right angles, and the proposition holds.

**Step 3.** Suppose angle ABC is not equal to angle ABD. From the point B, draw BE at right angles to CD [1.11]. Then each of the angles EBC and EBD is a right angle [D1.10].

**Step 4.** Now the angle EBC is equal to the sum of the angles EBA and ABC, since angle EBC is the whole and angles EBA and ABC are its parts [CN5, as the whole equals its parts taken together].

**Step 5.** Adding angle ABD to each side, the angles EBC and ABD together are equal to the angles EBA, ABC, and ABD together [CN2].

**Step 6.** Again, the angle ABD is equal to the sum of the angles ABE and EBD, since angle ABD is the whole and angles ABE and EBD are its parts.

**Step 7.** Adding angle ABC to each side, the angles ABD and ABC together are equal to the angles ABE, EBD, and ABC together [CN2].

**Step 8.** But it was shown in Step 5 that the angles EBC and ABD together are equal to the angles EBA, ABC, and ABD together, that is, to the angles ABE, ABC, and ABD together. And in Step 7 that the angles ABC and ABD together are equal to the angles ABC, ABE, and EBD together.

**Step 9.** Therefore the angles ABC and ABD together are equal to the angles EBC and EBD together [CN1], since both sums equal the same three-angle sum (angles ABC, ABE, and EBD).

**Step 10.** But angles EBC and EBD are two right angles [Step 3]. Therefore the angles ABC and ABD together are equal to two right angles.

**Step 11.** Therefore, if a straight line set up on a straight line makes angles, it will make either two right angles or angles equal to two right angles. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.14
**Statement:** If with any straight line, and at a point on it, two straight lines not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles, the two straight lines will be in a straight line with one another.

**Step 1.** Let there be a straight line AB, and at the point B on it, let two straight lines BC and BD, not lying on the same side of AB, make the adjacent angles ABC and ABD equal to two right angles. I say that BD is in a straight line with BC.

**Step 2.** Suppose BD is not in a straight line with BC. Then produce BC in a straight line to a point E, so that CBE is a straight line [P2].

**Step 3.** Since the straight line AB stands on the straight line CBE, the angles ABC and ABE are equal to two right angles [1.13].

**Step 4.** But the angles ABC and ABD are also equal to two right angles, by hypothesis.

**Step 5.** Therefore the angles ABC and ABE are equal to the angles ABC and ABD, since each sum is equal to two right angles [CN1].

**Step 6.** Subtract the angle ABC from each sum. Then the remaining angle ABE is equal to the remaining angle ABD [CN3].

**Step 7.** But angle ABE is the greater and angle ABD is the less, since BD falls between BA and BE, making ABD a part of ABE. Thus the whole would equal the part, which is impossible [CN5].

**Step 8.** Therefore BD is not not in a straight line with BC; that is, BD is in a straight line with BC, which was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.15
**Statement:** If two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let the two straight lines AB and CD cut one another at the point E. We must show that angle AEC equals angle DEB, and angle CEB equals angle AED.

**Step 2.** Since AEB is a straight line, and the straight line CE stands on it at E, by Proposition 1.13 the angles AEC and CEB together equal two right angles.

**Step 3.** Since CED is a straight line, and the straight line BE stands on it at E, by Proposition 1.13 the angles CEB and BED together equal two right angles.

**Step 4.** From Steps 2 and 3, the sum of angles AEC and CEB equals the sum of angles CEB and BED, since each sum equals two right angles [CN1].

**Step 5.** Subtracting the angle CEB, which is common to both sums, from each side, the remaining angle AEC equals the remaining angle BED [CN3].

**Step 6.** Similarly, since CED is a straight line, and the straight line AE stands on it at E, by Proposition 1.13 the angles CEA and AED together equal two right angles.

**Step 7.** From Steps 2 and 6, the sum of angles AEC and CEB equals the sum of angles CEA and AED, since each sum equals two right angles [CN1].

**Step 8.** Subtracting the angle AEC (which is the same as angle CEA), which is common to both sums, from each side, the remaining angle CEB equals the remaining angle AED [CN3].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if two straight lines cut one another, they make the vertical angles equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.16
**Statement:** In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and let the side BC be produced to D. We must show that the exterior angle ACD is greater than each of the interior and opposite angles BAC and ABC.

**Step 2.** Bisect AC at its midpoint E [1.10].

**Step 3.** Join B to E [P1] and produce the straight line BE to a point F beyond E [P2].

**Step 4.** Cut off EF equal to BE on the produced line [1.3].

**Step 5.** Join F to C [P1].

**Step 6.** In triangles AEB and CEF, we have AE = EC (since E is the midpoint of AC), BE = EF (by construction), and angle AEB = angle CEF (for the straight lines AC and BF cut one another at E, making the vertical angles equal) [1.15].

**Step 7.** Therefore, by the side-angle-side criterion, triangle AEB is congruent to triangle CEF, and in particular angle BAE = angle ECF [1.4].

**Step 8.** Now angle ACD is the whole angle at C on the side of D, and angle ECF is a part of angle ACD (since F lies within the region of angle ACD, as E is between A and C and F is on the extension of BE beyond E to the opposite side of line AC from B). Therefore angle ACD is greater than angle ECF [CN5].

**Step 9.** Since angle BAE is the same as angle BAC, and angle BAE = angle ECF (Step 7), and angle ACD > angle ECF (Step 8), we conclude that angle ACD is greater than angle BAC.

## Proposition 1.17
**Statement:** In any triangle two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles.

**Step 5.** Since angle ACD > angle ABC (Step 3), substituting the lesser angle ABC for the greater angle ACD in the sum yields angle ACB + angle ABC < angle ACB + angle ACD. But angle ACB + angle ACD equals two right angles (Step 4). Therefore angle ACB + angle ABC < two right angles.

**Step 6.** Again, by 1.16, the exterior angle ACD is also greater than the interior and opposite angle BAC. That is, angle ACD > angle BAC.

**Step 7.** Since angle ACD > angle BAC (Step 6), substituting the lesser angle BAC for the greater angle ACD gives angle ACB + angle BAC < angle ACB + angle ACD = two right angles. Therefore angle ACB + angle BAC < two right angles.

**Step 8.** Now produce side AB to point E [P2]. Then angle CBE is the exterior angle of triangle ABC formed by producing side AB.

**Step 9.** By 1.16, the exterior angle CBE is greater than the interior and opposite angle BAC. That is, angle CBE > angle BAC.

**Step 10.** By 1.13, since the straight line BC stands on the straight line AE, the angles ABC and CBE together equal two right angles. That is, angle ABC + angle CBE = two right angles.

**Step 11.** Since angle CBE > angle BAC (Step 9), substituting the lesser angle BAC for the greater angle CBE gives angle ABC + angle BAC < angle ABC + angle CBE = two right angles. Therefore angle ABC + angle BAC < two right angles.

**Step 12.** We have now shown that each of the three possible pairs of angles in triangle ABC — namely angles ACB and ABC (Step 5), angles ACB and BAC (Step 7), and angles ABC and BAC (Step 11) — sums to less than two right angles. Therefore, in any triangle, two angles taken together in any manner are less than two right angles. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.19
**Statement:** In any triangle the greater angle is subtended by the greater side.

**Step 5.** Since AC is neither equal to AB nor less than AB, it follows that AC is greater than AB. Therefore the greater angle ABC is subtended by the greater side AC.

## Proposition 1.21
**Statement:** If on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed will be less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but will contain a greaterangle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and on side BC, from its extremities B and C, let two straight lines BD and CD be constructed meeting at a point D within the triangle. I say that BD + DC < BA + AC, and that angle BDC > angle BAC.

**Step 5.** Now consider triangle DEC. By Proposition 1.20, any two sides of a triangle taken together are greater than the remaining side. Therefore DE + EC > DC.

**Step 6.** Adding BD to both sides of the inequality DE + EC > DC, we obtain BD + DE + EC > BD + DC. But BD + DE = BE, since D lies on segment BE. Therefore BE + EC > BD + DC.

**Step 7.** From Step 4 we have BA + AC > BE + EC, and from Step 6 we have BE + EC > BD + DC. Therefore BA + AC > BD + DC. That is, the two straight lines BD, DC constructed within the triangle are together less than the remaining two sides BA, AC of the triangle.

**Step 8.** Now for the angles. Since B, D, E are collinear and D lies between B and E, the angle BDC is an exterior angle of triangle CDE at vertex D. By Proposition 1.16, an exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the interior and opposite angles. Therefore angle BDC > angle CED.

**Step 9.** Since E lies on segment AC, and BE meets AC at E, the angle BEC (which is the same as angle CED from Step 8, since D lies on segment BE) is an exterior angle of triangle ABE at vertex E, formed by producing side AE of triangle ABE beyond E to C. By Proposition 1.16, angle BEC > angle BAE. But angle BAE is the same as angle BAC.

**Step 10.** From Step 8 we have angle BDC > angle BEC, and from Step 9 we have angle BEC > angle BAC. Therefore angle BDC > angle BAC. That is, the straight lines BD, DC contain a greater angle than the angle BAC.

Therefore, if on one of the sides of a triangle, from its extremities, there be constructed two straight lines meeting within the triangle, the straight lines so constructed are less than the remaining two sides of the triangle, but contain a greater angle. Q.E.F.

**Statement:** If two triangles have the two sides equal to two sides respectively, but have the one of the angles contained by the equal straight lines greater than the other, they will also have the base greater than the base.

**Step 8.** If F lies on segment EG, then since F is distinct from G (because rays DF and DG are distinct and DF = DG), we have EG = EF + FG with FG greater than zero, so EG is greater than EF, the whole being greater than its part. The conclusion BC greater than EF then follows from Step 5, and the proof is complete. [CN5]

**Step 9.** Assume now that F does not lie on segment EG, so that E, F, G form a proper triangle. We shall show that angle EFG is greater than angle EGF. Produce line DF beyond F to a point H. [P2]

**Step 10.** The straight line FE stands on line DH at point F, so angle DFE and angle EFH together equal two right angles. Since G lies on the opposite side of line DH from E (Step 7), the straight line FG likewise stands on line DH at F, so angle DFG and angle GFH together equal two right angles. [1.13]

**Step 11.** **(Case I: F falls within triangle DEG.)** Since E and G are on opposite sides of line DH at F, and F lies inside the triangle, ray FH (the extension of DF away from D) passes between rays FE and FG within the angle EFG. Therefore angle EFG = angle EFH + angle HFG = (two right angles minus angle DFE) + (two right angles minus angle DFG) = four right angles minus angle DFE minus angle DFG. At vertex G, since F is inside triangle DEG, ray GF lies between rays GD and GE, so angle EGF = angle DGE minus angle DGF. Applying angle DFG = angle DGF from Step 6, the difference angle EFG minus angle EGF equals four right angles minus angle DFE minus angle DGE. Now, in triangle DEF, any two angles taken together are less than two right angles, so in particular angle DFE is less than two right angles. [1.17] Similarly, in triangle DEG, angle DGE is less than two right angles. [1.17] Therefore their sum is less than four right angles, making the difference positive: angle EFG is greater than angle EGF.

**Step 12.** **(Case II: F falls outside triangle DEG, on the opposite side of segment EG from D.)** At vertex G, since D and F lie on opposite sides of line EG, angle DGF = angle DGE + angle EGF. Since angle EGF is a part of angle DGF, angle DGF is greater than angle EGF. [CN5] Since angle DGF = angle DFG (Step 6), angle DFG is greater than angle EGF. At vertex F, since D lies on the opposite side of line EG from F, ray FD passes between rays FE and FG within the angle EFG, so angle EFG = angle EFD + angle DFG. Since angle DFG is a part of angle EFG, angle EFG is greater than angle DFG. [CN5] Combining: angle EFG is greater than angle DFG, which is greater than angle EGF. Therefore angle EFG is greater than angle EGF.

**Step 13.** In both cases, angle EFG is greater than angle EGF in triangle EFG. Therefore the side opposite the greater angle is greater than the side opposite the lesser angle: EG is greater than EF. [1.19]

**Step 14.** Since BC = EG (Step 5), BC is greater than EF, which is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 1.27
**Statement:** If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the alternate angles equal to one another, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF fall on the two straight lines AB and CD, making the alternate angles AEF and EFD equal to one another. We must show that AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** Suppose, for the sake of contradiction, that AB and CD are not parallel. Then by definition D1.23, they will meet when produced in one direction or the other. Suppose they meet at a point G on the side of B and D, so that E, F, and G form a triangle EFG.

**Step 3.** In triangle EFG, the side EF is produced beyond E to A. Therefore angle AEF is an exterior angle of triangle EFG, and angle EFG (which is the same as angle EFD) is an interior and opposite angle of the same triangle.

**Step 4.** By Proposition 1.16, the exterior angle AEF of triangle EFG is greater than the interior and opposite angle EFG (that is, angle EFD).

**Step 5.** But angle AEF was assumed equal to angle EFD. Thus angle AEF is both greater than and equal to angle EFD, which is a contradiction.

**Step 6.** If instead we suppose AB and CD meet on the side of A and C at a point G', then triangle EFG' is formed. The angle EFD is an exterior angle of triangle EFG' (since DF is produced beyond F to G' through C), and angle FEA — but by symmetric reasoning, angle EFD would be greater than angle AEF by 1.16, again contradicting the hypothesis that they are equal.

**Step 7.** Since the assumption that AB and CD meet leads to a contradiction in either direction, AB and CD do not meet when produced indefinitely. Therefore, by definition D1.23, AB is parallel to CD.

## Proposition 1.28
**Statement:** If a straight line falling on two straight lines make the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines will be parallel to one another.

**Step 1.** Let the straight line EF, falling on two straight lines AB and CD, make either (a) the exterior angle EGB equal to the interior and opposite angle GHD on the same side, or (b) the interior angles BGH and GHD on the same side equal to two right angles. We prove that in each case AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 2.** [Case (a)] Suppose angle EGB equals angle GHD. Since lines AB and EF intersect at G, by 1.15 the vertical angles EGB and AGH are equal, that is, angle EGB equals angle AGH.

**Step 3.** Since angle EGB equals angle GHD (hypothesis) and angle EGB equals angle AGH (Step 2), by CN1 angle AGH equals angle GHD.

**Step 4.** But angles AGH and GHD are alternate angles formed by the transversal EF falling on lines AB and CD. Since they are equal, by 1.27 the straight lines AB and CD are parallel to one another.

**Step 5.** [Case (b)] Now suppose the interior angles on the same side, BGH and GHD, are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 6.** Since the straight line EF stands on the straight line AB at G, by 1.13 the adjacent angles EGB and BGH are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 7.** But angles BGH and GHD are also together equal to two right angles (hypothesis). Therefore by CN1, angle EGB plus angle BGH equals angle BGH plus angle GHD.

**Step 8.** Subtracting the common angle BGH from each sum, by CN3 angle EGB equals angle GHD.

**Step 9.** But angle EGB is the exterior angle and angle GHD is the interior and opposite angle on the same side. This is exactly the condition of Case (a). Therefore by Steps 2 through 4 (using 1.15, CN1, and 1.27), AB is parallel to CD.

**Step 10.** Therefore, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, or the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles, the straight lines are parallel to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.29
**Statement:** A straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles.

We must show three things: (i) the alternate angles AGH and GHD are equal, (ii) the exterior angle EGB equals the interior and opposite angle GHD, and (iii) the interior angles on the same side BGH and GHD are together equal to two right angles.

**Step 2.** (Part i) Suppose, for contradiction, that the alternate angles AGH and GHD are not equal. Then one of them is greater than the other. Suppose angle AGH is greater than angle GHD.

**Step 3.** Add angle BGH to each. Then angle AGH together with angle BGH is greater than angle GHD together with angle BGH [CN5 — the whole (AGH + BGH) is greater than the part (GHD + BGH) since AGH > GHD implies AGH + BGH > GHD + BGH].

**Step 5.** Therefore the angles BGH and GHD are together less than two right angles [from Steps 3 and 4].

**Step 6.** But straight lines which are met by a transversal making the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, if produced indefinitely, meet on that side [P5]. Therefore AB and CD, if produced, meet on the side of B and D.

**Step 7.** But AB and CD are parallel, and therefore do not meet [D1.23]. This is a contradiction.

**Step 8.** Therefore the assumption that angle AGH is not equal to angle GHD is false. By the same argument, angle GHD cannot be greater than angle AGH. Therefore the alternate angles AGH and GHD are equal.

**Step 9.** (Part ii) Now, angle AGH is equal to angle EGB, since they are vertical angles formed by the two straight lines AB and EF cutting one another at G [1.15].

**Step 10.** Since angle AGH equals angle GHD [Step 8] and angle AGH equals angle EGB [Step 9], it follows that angle EGB equals angle GHD [CN1]. That is, the exterior angle EGB equals the interior and opposite angle GHD.

**Step 11.** (Part iii) Add angle BGH to each of the equal angles EGB and GHD. Then angle EGB together with angle BGH equals angle GHD together with angle BGH [CN2].

**Step 12.** But angles EGB and BGH are together equal to two right angles, since the straight line EF stands on the straight line AB [1.13].

**Step 13.** Therefore angles BGH and GHD are together equal to two right angles [CN1, from Steps 11 and 12].

**Step 14.** Therefore a straight line falling on parallel straight lines makes the alternate angles equal to one another, the exterior angle equal to the interior and opposite angle on the same side, and the interior angles on the same side equal to two right angles. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.32
**Statement:** In any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a triangle, and let side BC be produced to D [P2]. We must show that the exterior angle ACD equals the sum of the two interior and opposite angles CAB and ABC, and that the three interior angles ABC, BCA, and CAB together equal two right angles.

**Step 2.** Through point C, draw CE parallel to the straight line AB [1.31].

**Step 3.** Since AB is parallel to CE, and AC is a straight line falling on them, the alternate angles BAC and ACE are equal to one another [1.29]. That is, angle ACE equals angle BAC.

**Step 4.** Again, since AB is parallel to CE, and the straight line BD falls on them, the exterior angle ECD is equal to the interior and opposite angle ABC on the same side [1.29]. That is, angle ECD equals angle ABC.

**Step 5.** But angle ACE was shown equal to angle BAC (Step 3), and angle ECD was shown equal to angle ABC (Step 4). Therefore the whole angle ACD, which is the sum of angles ACE and ECD, equals the sum of angles BAC and ABC [CN2]. This is the first part of the proposition: the exterior angle ACD equals the two interior and opposite angles.

**Step 6.** Now add angle ACB to both sides. The angles ACD and ACB together equal the angles ABC, BAC, and ACB together [CN2].

**Step 7.** But angles ACD and ACB are the angles made by the straight line AC standing on the straight line BD; therefore angles ACD and ACB together equal two right angles [1.13].

**Step 8.** Therefore the three interior angles ABC, BCA, and BAC are together equal to two right angles [CN1]. This is the second part of the proposition.

Therefore, in any triangle, if one of the sides be produced, the exterior angle is equal to the two interior and opposite angles, and the three interior angles of the triangle are equal to two right angles. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 1.34
**Statement:** In parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a parallelogrammic area with AB parallel to DC and AD parallel to BC. Let AC be a diameter (diagonal) of it.

**Step 2.** Since AB is parallel to DC, and the straight line AC falls upon them, the alternate angles BAC and DCA are equal to one another. [1.29]

**Step 3.** Since AD is parallel to BC, and the straight line AC falls upon them, the alternate angles DAC and BCA are equal to one another. [1.29]

**Step 4.** In triangles ABC and CDA, we have: angle BAC equals angle DCA (Step 2), angle BCA equals angle DAC (Step 3), and the side AC between these angles is common to both triangles. Therefore by Proposition 1.26 (ASA), triangle ABC is equal to triangle CDA, and the remaining sides equal the remaining sides respectively: AB equals CD, and BC equals DA. [1.26]

**Step 5.** Thus the opposite sides of the parallelogram are equal to one another: AB equals CD, and BC equals DA.

**Step 6.** Since angle BAC equals angle DCA (Step 2) and angle DAC equals angle BCA (Step 3), adding equals to equals, the whole angle BAD equals the whole angle DCB. [CN2]

**Step 7.** Since AB is parallel to DC and the transversal BC falls upon them, the interior angles on the same side are together equal to two right angles: angle ABC plus angle DCB equals two right angles. [1.29] Likewise, since AD is parallel to BC and the transversal DC falls upon them, the interior angles on the same side are together equal to two right angles: angle ADC plus angle DCB equals two right angles. [1.29]

**Step 8.** Since angle ABC plus angle DCB equals two right angles, and angle ADC plus angle DCB also equals two right angles, we have angle ABC plus angle DCB equals angle ADC plus angle DCB. Therefore angle ABC equals angle ADC. [CN1, CN3]

**Step 9.** Thus the opposite angles of the parallelogram are equal to one another: angle BAD equals angle DCB, and angle ABC equals angle ADC.

**Step 10.** Finally, the diameter AC bisects the parallelogram ABCD, since triangle ABC was proved equal to triangle CDA in Step 4.

**Step 11.** Therefore, in parallelogrammic areas the opposite sides and angles are equal to one another, and the diameter bisects the areas. Q.E.D.

**Step 8.** Thus in triangles EAB and FDC: the two sides EA, AB are equal to the two sides FD, DC respectively (EA equals FD by Step 5, and AB equals DC by Step 6), and the included angle EAB is equal to the included angle FDC (by Step 7). **Step 9.** Let G be the point of intersection of lines BE and CD. The triangle DGE is a common part of both triangle EAB and triangle FDC. Subtracting triangle DGE from triangle EAB yields the trapezium ABGD, and subtracting triangle DGE from triangle FDC yields the trapezium EGCF. ## Proposition 1.37
**Statement:** Triangles which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABC and DBC be two triangles on the same base BC and in the same parallels BC and AD. We are to prove that triangle ABC equals triangle DBC.

**Step 2.** Through B, draw BE parallel to CA, meeting line DA produced at E [1.31]. Through C, draw CF parallel to BD, meeting line AD produced at F [1.31].

**Step 3.** Since BE is parallel to AC (by construction) and BC is parallel to EA (because A and E both lie on line AD, which is parallel to BC by hypothesis), the quadrilateral EBCA is a parallelogram [D1.22].

**Step 4.** Since CF is parallel to BD (by construction) and BC is parallel to DF (because D and F both lie on line AD, which is parallel to BC by hypothesis), the quadrilateral DBCF is a parallelogram [D1.22].

**Step 5.** The parallelograms EBCA and DBCF are on the same base BC and in the same parallels BC and EF (since E, A, D, F all lie on line AD, which is parallel to BC). Therefore parallelogram EBCA equals parallelogram DBCF [1.35].

**Step 6.** The diagonal AB of parallelogram EBCA bisects it, so triangle ABC is half of parallelogram EBCA [1.34].

**Step 7.** The diagonal DC of parallelogram DBCF bisects it, so triangle DBC is half of parallelogram DBCF [1.34].

**Step 8.** Since parallelogram EBCA equals parallelogram DBCF (Step 5), and triangle ABC is half of EBCA (Step 6), and triangle DBC is half of DBCF (Step 7), the halves of equal things are equal. Therefore triangle ABC equals triangle DBC [CN3].

**Step 9.** Therefore, triangles which are on the same base and in the same parallels are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.43
**Statement:** In any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be a parallelogram, and AC its diameter. Let EH and FG be straight lines drawn through a point K on AC, parallel to the sides of the parallelogram, where EH is parallel to AB and DC, and FG is parallel to AD and BC. Then the parallelograms about the diameter are AEKH (with diameter AK) and KGCF (with diameter KC), and their complements are EBGK and HKFD. We are to prove that complement EBGK equals complement HKFD.

**Step 2.** Since ABCD is a parallelogram and AC is its diameter, by 1.34 the diameter AC bisects the parallelogram ABCD. Therefore triangle ABC is equal to triangle ACD.

**Step 3.** Since AEKH is a parallelogram and AK is its diameter, by 1.34 the diameter AK bisects the parallelogram AEKH. Therefore triangle AEK is equal to triangle AHK.

**Step 4.** Since KGCF is a parallelogram and KC is its diameter, by 1.34 the diameter KC bisects the parallelogram KGCF. Therefore triangle KGC is equal to triangle KFC.

**Step 5.** Now, triangle ABC is composed of triangle AEK, triangle KGC, and complement EBGK. That is, triangle ABC equals triangle AEK plus triangle KGC plus complement EBGK.

**Step 6.** Similarly, triangle ACD is composed of triangle AHK, triangle KFC, and complement HKFD. That is, triangle ACD equals triangle AHK plus triangle KFC plus complement HKFD.

**Step 7.** From Step 2, triangle ABC equals triangle ACD. From Step 3, triangle AEK equals triangle AHK. From Step 4, triangle KGC equals triangle KFC. Since triangle AEK equals triangle AHK and triangle KGC equals triangle KFC, the sum triangle AEK plus triangle KGC equals the sum triangle AHK plus triangle KFC, by CN2.

**Step 8.** Since triangle ABC equals triangle ACD (Step 2), and triangle AEK plus triangle KGC equals triangle AHK plus triangle KFC (Step 7), subtracting the latter equals from the former equals, by CN3, the remainders are equal. That is, complement EBGK equals complement HKFD.

**Step 9.** Therefore, in any parallelogram the complements of the parallelograms about the diameter are equal to one another. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 1.45
**Statement:** To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure.

**Step 1.** Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure (a quadrilateral; the argument generalizes to any polygon by drawing additional diagonals), and let angle E be the given rectilineal angle. Draw the diagonal DB, dividing ABCD into triangles ABD and DBC [P1].

Since FGHK is a parallelogram, FK is parallel to GH, and the transversal KH falling on these parallels makes the co-interior angles FKH and KHG equal to two right angles [1.29]. Since angle FKH equals angle E (Step 2) and angle GHM equals angle E (Step 3), we have angle FKH equals angle GHM. Therefore angle KHG plus angle GHM equals angle KHG plus angle FKH equals two right angles. Since the adjacent angles KHG and GHM on the same side of the line GH at the point H sum to two right angles, KHM is a straight line [1.14].

**Step 5.** Since KHM is a straight line, the line GH meets the straight line KM, making angles GHK and GHM on opposite sides. Therefore angle GHK plus angle GHM equals two right angles [1.13].

**Step 6.** We show that FGL is a straight line. Since FGHK is a parallelogram, FG is parallel to KH, and the transversal GH falling on these parallels makes the co-interior angles FGH and GHK equal to two right angles [1.29]. Since GHLM is a parallelogram, GL is parallel to HM, and the transversal GH falling on these parallels makes the co-interior angles LGH and GHM equal to two right angles [1.29]. Therefore angle FGH plus angle LGH equals (two right angles minus angle GHK) plus (two right angles minus angle GHM) equals four right angles minus (angle GHK plus angle GHM). By Step 5, angle GHK plus angle GHM equals two right angles, so angle FGH plus angle LGH equals four right angles minus two right angles equals two right angles. Since the adjacent angles FGH and LGH at the point G sum to two right angles, FGL is a straight line [1.14].

**Step 7.** Since FGHK is a parallelogram, FK is parallel to GH. Since GHLM is a parallelogram, GH is parallel to LM. Therefore FK is parallel to LM, since both are parallel to GH [1.30].

**Step 8.** Since FGL and KHM are both straight lines (Steps 4 and 6), and FG is parallel to KH (from parallelogram FGHK), the straight line FL is parallel to the straight line KM. Together with FK parallel to LM (Step 7), the figure FKML has both pairs of opposite sides parallel, so FKML is a parallelogram.

**Step 9.** Since FGL and KHM are straight lines, the parallelogram FKML is composed of parallelograms FGHK and GHLM. But triangle ABD plus triangle DBC equals the whole figure ABCD, since diagonal DB divides ABCD into exactly these two triangles. Therefore parallelogram FKML equals the rectilineal figure ABCD [CN2].

**Step 10.** The angle FKM of the parallelogram FKML equals angle FKH (since KHM is a straight line, so the ray KH is the same as the ray KM from K), which equals angle E by construction (Step 2).

**Step 11.** Therefore parallelogram FKML has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure ABCD, in the given angle E. For a polygon of more than four sides, draw further diagonals to decompose it into additional triangles, and repeat the application step (Step 3) using 1.44 for each successive triangle; the same argument at each stage shows the sides align into straight lines and the resulting figure is a parallelogram equal to the whole given figure in the given angle. **Step 9.** The square BAGF is double of triangle FBC, since they are on the same base FB and in the same parallels FB and GC (for BA and AH are in a straight line by Step 5, and since BAGF is a square, GF is parallel to BA; also GC is the line from G to C, but more precisely: the square BAGF and triangle FBC share the base FB, and the vertex C of the triangle and the side AG of the square lie in the same parallel to FB, namely the line through G and A and C, since GA is a side of the square parallel to FB by construction, and A, G, C are connected through the collinearity of CA and AG from Step 4). Therefore the square BAGF is double of triangle FBC [1.41].

**Statement:** If in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right.

**Step 6.** But the square on DC is equal to the squares on DA and AC, for the angle DAC is right [1.47].

**Step 7.** And the square on BC is equal to the squares on BA and AC, for this is given by hypothesis.

**Step 8.** Therefore the square on DC is equal to the square on BC [CN1].

**Step 10.** Now since DA is equal to AB, AC is common, and DC is equal to BC, the two sides DA, AC are equal to the two sides BA, AC respectively, and the base DC is equal to the base BC.

**Step 11.** Therefore the angle DAC is equal to the angle BAC [1.8].

**Step 12.** But the angle DAC is right. Therefore the angle BAC is also right.

**Step 13.** Therefore, if in a triangle the square on one of the sides be equal to the squares on the remaining two sides of the triangle, the angle contained by the remaining two sides of the triangle is right. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.1
**Statement:** If there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments.

We must show that the rectangle contained by A and BC is equal to the rectangle contained by A and BD, together with the rectangle contained by A and DE, and the rectangle contained by A and EC.

**Step 3.** Through G, draw GH parallel to BC [1.31]. Through D, E, and C, draw DK, EL, and CH parallel to BG, meeting GH at K, L, and H respectively [1.31].

**Step 4.** Now BGKD is a parallelogram, for BG is parallel to DK (by construction) and GK is parallel to BD (since GK is part of GH which is parallel to BC). Since the angle GBD is a right angle (by construction in Step 2), BGKD is a rectangle. Moreover, BG is equal to A (by construction). Therefore, by the definition of a rectangular parallelogram [D2.1], BGKD is the rectangle contained by A and BD.

**Step 5.** Similarly, DKLE is a parallelogram with DK parallel to EL and KL parallel to DE. Since DK is parallel to BG and BG is perpendicular to BC, DK is also perpendicular to BC [1.29], so the angle KDE is a right angle. Therefore DKLE is a rectangle. Now DK is equal to BG [1.34], and BG is equal to A, so DK is equal to A. Therefore DKLE is the rectangle contained by A and DE [D2.1].

**Step 6.** Similarly, ELHC is a rectangle. EL is equal to BG [1.34], and BG is equal to A, so EL is equal to A. Therefore ELHC is the rectangle contained by A and EC [D2.1].

**Step 7.** Now BGHC is the rectangle contained by A and BC, since BG equals A and BC is the base [D2.1], and the angle at B is a right angle.

**Step 8.** The rectangle BGHC is made up of the rectangles BGKD, DKLE, and ELHC. Therefore the rectangle contained by A and BC is equal to the rectangle contained by A and BD, together with the rectangle contained by A and DE, and the rectangle contained by A and EC [CN2].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if there be two straight lines, and one of them be cut into any number of segments whatever, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines is equal to the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.2
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and both of the segments is equal to the square on the whole.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C, so that the segments are AC and CB. We are to show that the rectangle contained by AB and AC together with the rectangle contained by AB and CB is equal to the square on AB.

**Step 2.** Consider two straight lines, both equal to AB. Let one of them be cut at the point C into the segments AC and CB. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by the two straight lines (that is, the rectangle contained by AB and AB) is equal to the sum of the rectangles contained by the uncut straight line and each of the segments; that is, rect(AB, AB) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB). [2.1]

**Step 3.** Now, the rectangle contained by AB and AB is the rectangle contained by two equal straight lines meeting at a right angle, which by Definition D2.1 (a rectangular parallelogram is contained by the two straight lines containing the right angle) and Definition D1.22 (a square is both equilateral and right-angled) is the square on AB. That is, rect(AB, AB) = sq(AB). [D2.1, D1.22]

**Step 4.** Substituting into the equality from Step 2, we obtain: sq(AB) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB). [CN1]

**Step 5.** Therefore, the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment AC, together with the rectangle contained by the whole AB and the segment CB, is equal to the square on AB. This is what was to be proved.

## Proposition 2.3
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the rectangle contained by the segments and the square on the aforesaid segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. We are to show that the rectangle contained by AB and BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on BC.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB has been cut at the point C, it is divided into the segments AC and CB.

**Step 3.** Take BC as a separate straight line, and consider AB as a straight line cut into the segments AC and CB. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by BC and AB is equal to the rectangle contained by BC and AC together with the rectangle contained by BC and CB. That is, rect(BC, AB) = rect(BC, AC) + rect(BC, CB).

**Step 4.** Now the rectangle contained by BC and CB is the rectangle contained by two equal straight lines, both equal to BC. By the definition of a square (D1.22), a square is a quadrilateral that is both equilateral and right-angled; the square on BC is precisely the rectangle contained by BC and BC (D2.1). ## Proposition 2.4
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole is equal to the squares on the segments and twice the rectangle contained by the segments.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. We are to show that the square on AB equals the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB.

**Step 2.** Since AB is cut at C, by Proposition 2.2, the square on AB is equal to the sum of the rectangle contained by AB and AC together with the rectangle contained by AB and CB. That is, sq(AB) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB).

**Step 3.** Since AB is cut at C, apply Proposition 2.3 taking AC as the aforesaid segment. Then the rectangle contained by AB and AC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on AC. That is, rect(AB, AC) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(AC).

**Step 4.** Again, since AB is cut at C, apply Proposition 2.3 taking CB as the aforesaid segment. Then the rectangle contained by AB and CB is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and CB together with the square on CB. That is, rect(AB, CB) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB).

**Step 5.** From Step 2, sq(AB) = rect(AB, AC) + rect(AB, CB). Substituting the equals established in Steps 3 and 4 by Common Notion 1, we obtain sq(AB) = rect(AC, CB) + sq(AC) + rect(AC, CB) + sq(CB).

**Step 6.** Collecting terms by Common Notion 2, this gives sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(CB) + 2*rect(AC, CB). Therefore the square on the whole AB is equal to the squares on the segments AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB, which was to be proved.

Note: This proof takes an algebraic route via 2.2 and 2.3 rather than Euclid's geometric construction (which builds the square on AB, draws the diagonal, constructs parallels, and identifies sub-squares and complements using 1.43, 1.46, etc.). The algebraic path is more direct, requiring fewer steps and fewer citations.

## Proposition 2.5
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the rectangle contained by the unequal segments of the whole together with the square on the straight line between the points of section is equal to the square on the half.

**Step 1.** Let AB be the given straight line cut into equal segments at C, so that AC equals CB, and cut into unequal segments at D (with D between C and B, without loss of generality). We are to prove that the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CD equals the square on CB.

**Step 2.** Since CB is cut at D, by Proposition 2.3 the rectangle contained by CB and DB equals the rectangle contained by CD and DB together with the square on DB. That is, rect(CB, DB) = rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB).

**Step 3.** Since AD is composed of AC and CD, and AC equals CB (because C bisects AB), it follows that AD equals CB together with CD. By Common Notion 2, since AC = CB, we have AD = AC + CD = CB + CD.

**Step 4.** Consider the rectangle contained by AD and DB. Since AD equals the sum of CB and CD (Step 3), the line AD is cut into segments CB and CD. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by AD and DB equals the rectangle contained by CB and DB together with the rectangle contained by CD and DB. That is, rect(AD, DB) = rect(CB, DB) + rect(CD, DB).

**Step 5.** Substituting the result of Step 2 into Step 4: rect(AD, DB) = [rect(CD, DB) + sq(DB)] + rect(CD, DB). Therefore rect(AD, DB) = sq(DB) + 2*rect(CD, DB).

**Step 6.** Now consider the square on CB. Since CB is cut at D into segments CD and DB, by Proposition 2.4, the square on CB equals the squares on CD and DB together with twice the rectangle contained by CD and DB. That is, sq(CB) = sq(CD) + sq(DB) + 2*rect(CD, DB).

**Step 7.** From Step 5, sq(DB) + 2*rect(CD, DB) = rect(AD, DB). Substituting this into Step 6: sq(CB) = sq(CD) + rect(AD, DB).

**Step 8.** Therefore the rectangle contained by AD and DB together with the square on CD equals the square on CB. By Common Notion 1 (applied in the substitution equalities throughout), this is what was to be proved. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 2.6
**Statement:** If a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line bisected at C, and let BD be added to it in a straight line. We must show that the rectangle AD·BD together with the square on CB equals the square on CD.

**Step 2.** Since AB is bisected at C, we have AC = CB. The line AD consists of AC, CB, and BD, so AD = AC + CB + BD. Since AC = CB, it follows that AD = AB + BD, where AB = AC + CB.

**Step 3.** Consider the straight line AD, which is cut at B into segments AB and BD. By Proposition 2.3, the rectangle contained by the whole AD and the segment BD equals the rectangle contained by the segments AB and BD together with the square on BD. That is, rect(AD, BD) = rect(AB, BD) + sq(BD).

**Step 4.** Now consider the straight line AB, which is cut at C into segments AC and CB. By Proposition 2.1, the rectangle contained by the uncut line BD and the whole AB equals the sum of the rectangles contained by BD and each segment. That is, rect(AB, BD) = rect(AC, BD) + rect(CB, BD).

**Step 5.** Since AC = CB (AB being bisected at C), by Common Notion 1, rect(AC, BD) = rect(CB, BD). Therefore rect(AB, BD) = rect(CB, BD) + rect(CB, BD) = 2·rect(CB, BD).

**Step 6.** Substituting back into Step 3: rect(AD, BD) = 2·rect(CB, BD) + sq(BD).

**Step 7.** Adding the square on CB to both sides (Common Notion 2): rect(AD, BD) + sq(CB) = 2·rect(CB, BD) + sq(BD) + sq(CB).

**Step 8.** Now consider the straight line CD, which equals CB + BD. By Proposition 2.4, the square on the whole CD equals the squares on CB and BD together with twice the rectangle contained by CB and BD. That is, sq(CD) = sq(CB) + sq(BD) + 2·rect(CB, BD).

**Step 9.** The right-hand side of Step 7 is sq(CB) + sq(BD) + 2·rect(CB, BD), which equals sq(CD) by Step 8 and Common Notion 1. Therefore rect(AD, BD) + sq(CB) = sq(CD).

**Step 10.** Therefore, if a straight line be bisected and a straight line be added to it in a straight line, the rectangle contained by the whole with the added straight line and the added straight line together with the square on the half is equal to the square on the straight line made up of the half and the added straight line. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 2.7
**Statement:** If a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and that on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment and the square on the remaining segment.

**Step 1.** Let AB be a straight line cut at random at the point C. We must show that the square on AB together with the square on BC equals twice the rectangle contained by AB and BC together with the square on AC.

**Step 2.** Since the straight line AB has been cut at random at C, by Proposition 2.4 the square on AB is equal to the squares on AC and CB together with twice the rectangle contained by AC and CB. That is, sq(AB) = sq(AC) + sq(BC) + 2·rect(AC,BC).

**Step 3.** Adding the square on BC to both sides, by Common Notion 2, sq(AB) + sq(BC) = sq(AC) + sq(BC) + sq(BC) + 2·rect(AC,BC) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(BC) + 2·rect(AC,BC).

**Step 4.** Since the straight line AB has been cut at random at C, by Proposition 2.3 the rectangle contained by AB and BC is equal to the rectangle contained by AC and BC together with the square on BC. That is, rect(AB,BC) = rect(AC,BC) + sq(BC).

**Step 5.** Therefore twice the rectangle contained by AB and BC equals twice the rectangle contained by AC and BC together with twice the square on BC, by Common Notion 2 applied to equal magnitudes doubled. That is, 2·rect(AB,BC) = 2·rect(AC,BC) + 2·sq(BC).

**Step 6.** Adding the square on AC to both sides, by Common Notion 2, 2·rect(AB,BC) + sq(AC) = 2·rect(AC,BC) + 2·sq(BC) + sq(AC).

**Step 7.** But from Step 3, sq(AB) + sq(BC) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(BC) + 2·rect(AC,BC), and from Step 6, 2·rect(AB,BC) + sq(AC) = sq(AC) + 2·sq(BC) + 2·rect(AC,BC). The right-hand sides are identical.

**Step 8.** Therefore, by Common Notion 1, sq(AB) + sq(BC) = 2·rect(AB,BC) + sq(AC).

**Step 9.** That is, if a straight line be cut at random, the square on the whole and the square on one of the segments both together are equal to twice the rectangle contained by the whole and the said segment together with the square on the remaining segment. Q.E.D.

**Step 5.** Now consider the straight line AB cut at C. By Proposition 2.7, the square on AB together with the square on CB is equal to twice the rectangle contained by AB and CB together with the square on AC. That is, sq(AB) + sq(CB) = 2*rect(AB, CB) + sq(AC) [2.7].

**Step 7.** Therefore four times the rectangle contained by AB and CB together with the square on AC is equal to the square on AD, that is, the square described on AB and CB as on one straight line. This is what was to be proved.

**Step 4.** Since CE is parallel to DF and GF is parallel to CD, the figure CGFD is a parallelogram. By 1.34, GF = CD and CG = DF. Also, opposite angles are equal, so angle GFD = angle GCD = a right angle (since CE is perpendicular to AB) [1.34].

**Step 5.** In triangle ACE, angle ACE is a right angle, and AC = CE by construction. Since the triangle is isosceles, angle CAE = angle CEA [1.5]. The sum of the angles equals two right angles [1.32], so angle ACE + angle CAE + angle CEA = two right angles. Since angle ACE is one right angle, angles CAE and CEA together equal one right angle, and since they are equal, each is half of a right angle.

**Step 6.** In triangle ECB, angle ECB is a right angle, and EC = CB (since EC = AC = CB). By the same reasoning as Step 5 [1.5, 1.32], angle CEB = angle CBE = half of a right angle.

**Step 7.** Therefore angle AEB = angle AEC + angle CEB = half a right angle + half a right angle = one right angle [CN2].

**Step 8.** Since G lies between C and E on line CE, and angle FGC is a right angle (from the parallelogram, Step 4), angle FGE is supplementary to angle FGC and therefore also a right angle [1.13].

**Step 9.** In triangle EGF, angle EGF is a right angle (Step 8), and angle GEF = angle CEB = half a right angle (since G is on CE and F is on EB, so angle GEF is the same angle as angle CEB, from Step 6). By 1.32, angle EGF + angle GEF + angle GFE = two right angles. So one right angle + half a right angle + angle GFE = two right angles, giving angle GFE = half a right angle.

**Step 10.** Since angle GEF = angle GFE = half a right angle, triangle EGF is isosceles with EG = GF [1.6]. But GF = CD [1.34, from Step 4]. Therefore EG = CD [CN1].

**Step 11.** Now, DF is parallel to CE, and CE is perpendicular to AB. Since parallel lines make equal corresponding angles with a transversal [1.29], DF is also perpendicular to AB. Thus angle FDA and angle FDB are each right angles.

**Step 12.** We show that DF = DB. From Step 4, DF = CG [1.34]. Now CG = CE - EG = AC - CD (since CE = AC and EG = CD from Steps 2 and 10) [CN3]. Also DB = CB - CD = AC - CD (since CB = AC). Therefore DF = DB [CN1].

**Step 14.** Apply 1.47 to the right triangle EGF (right angle at G): the square on EF equals the sum of the squares on EG and GF. Since EG = GF = CD (Step 10), the square on EF equals twice the square on CD [1.47].

**Step 15.** Since F lies on segment EB and angle AEB is a right angle (Step 7), angle AEF is also a right angle. Apply 1.47 to the right triangle AEF (right angle at E): the square on AF equals the sum of the squares on AE and EF. From Steps 13 and 14, the square on AF equals twice the square on AC together with twice the square on CD, that is, double of the square on AC and the square on CD [1.47, CN2].

**Step 16.** Apply 1.47 to the right triangle ADF (right angle at D, from Step 11): the square on AF equals the sum of the squares on AD and DF [1.47].

**Step 17.** From Steps 15 and 16, the sum of the squares on AD and DF equals double of the square on AC together with the square on CD [CN1]. Since DF = DB (Step 12), the square on DF equals the square on DB. Therefore the sum of the squares on AD and DB equals double of the square on AC together with the square on CD [CN1].

**Step 18.** Therefore, if a straight line be cut into equal and unequal segments, the squares on the unequal segments of the whole are double of the square on the half and of the square on the straight line between the points of section. Q.E.F.

## Proposition 2.11
**Statement:** To cut a given straight line so that the rectangle contained by the whole and one of the segments is equal to the square on the remaining segment.

**Step 5.** Construct the square FGHA on FA [1.46], so that FA = AG = GH = HF and all angles of FGHA are right. The point H falls on AB.

**Step 6.** We claim that H is the required point, i.e., that rect(AB, HB) = sq(AH).

**Step 12.** Substituting into the result of Step 10: rect(CA, FA) + sq(FA) = sq(AB).

**Step 13.** Since ABDC is a square, CA = AB. Since FGHA is a square, FA = AH and sq(FA) = sq(AH). Therefore: rect(AB, AH) + sq(AH) = sq(AB).

**Step 14.** Since H lies on AB, the line AB is cut at H into segments AH and HB. By Proposition 2.2: rect(AB, AH) + rect(AB, HB) = sq(AB).

**Statement:** In obtuse-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the obtuse angle is greater than the squares on the sides containing the obtuse angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the obtuse angle, namely that on which the   perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle.

That is, sq(AC) = sq(AD) + sq(DC) [1.47].

**Step 6.** Similarly, since the angle ADB is also a right angle (AD is perpendicular to the line BDC), in the right-angled triangle ADB with the right angle at D, by the Pythagorean theorem, the square on AB equals the sum of the squares on AD and DB. That is, sq(AB) = sq(AD) + sq(DB) [1.47].

**Step 7.** Substituting the results of Steps 5 and 6 into the equation from Step 4: the left side sq(DC) + sq(DA) equals sq(AC) by Step 5, and the term sq(DB) + sq(DA) on the right side equals sq(AB) by Step 6. Therefore, sq(AC) = sq(AB) + sq(BC) + 2*rect(BC, BD).

**Step 8.** This shows that in the obtuse-angled triangle ABC, the square on AC (the side subtending the obtuse angle) is greater than the squares on AB and BC (the sides containing the obtuse angle) by twice the rectangle contained by BC and BD, where BC is the side about the obtuse angle on which the perpendicular falls, and BD is the straight line cut off outside by the perpendicular towards the obtuse angle. **Statement:** In acute-angled triangles the square on the side subtending the acute angle is less than the squares on the sides containing the acute angle by twice the rectangle contained by one of the sides about the acute angle, namely that on which the perpendicular falls, and the straight line cut off within by the perpendicular towards the acute angle.

## Proposition 3.1
**Statement:** To find the centre of a given circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given circle. We wish to find its centre.

**Step 2.** Draw any chord AB in the circle [P1]. Bisect AB at the point D [1.10].

**Step 3.** From D, draw DC at right angles to AB [1.11]. Produce DC to meet the circle at E [P2]. Bisect CE at F [1.10].

**Step 4.** I say that F is the centre of the circle ABC. Suppose it is not. If possible, let G, a point not on CE, be the centre. Join GA, GD, and GB [P1].

**Step 5.** Since D is the midpoint of AB, we have DA = DB [D1.15, by construction in Step 2].

**Step 6.** Since G is assumed to be the centre of the circle, GA = GB [D1.15].

**Step 7.** In triangles GDA and GDB, we have DA = DB (Step 5), GA = GB (Step 6), and GD is common.

**Step 8.** Therefore triangle GDA is congruent to triangle GDB, and hence angle GDA = angle GDB [1.8].

**Step 9.** When a straight line standing on another straight line makes the adjacent angles equal to one another, each of the equal angles is a right angle [D1.10]. Therefore angle GDA is a right angle.

**Step 10.** But angle FDA is also a right angle, since DC was drawn at right angles to AB at D (Step 3).

**Step 11.** Therefore angle GDA = angle FDA [P4, since all right angles are equal].

**Step 12.** But angle GDA is a part of angle FDA (since G is not on line CE, the angle GDA is less than or equal to FDA only if G lies on the same side; however, if G is off the line CE, then one of these angles is a proper part of the other). Since they are equal, yet the whole equals the part, this contradicts CN5, which states that the whole is greater than the part.

**Step 13.** Therefore G cannot be the centre of the circle unless G lies on CE. Since the same argument applies for any point off the line CE, the centre must lie on CE.

**Step 14.** By the same construction, if we were to draw another chord and its perpendicular bisector, the centre would have to lie on that perpendicular bisector as well. But we can establish that F is the centre directly: since F is the midpoint of the diameter CE (a chord through the centre lies on CE by the argument above), F is equidistant from C and E, and any chord through F would be bisected by the perpendicular from F, which is the defining property of the centre.

**Step 15.** More precisely, suppose the centre is some other point F' on CE, with F' different from F. Since F' is the centre, F'C = F'E [D1.15]. But F is the midpoint of CE, so FC = FE. If F' is different from F and also on segment CE, then F'C and F'E cannot both be equal unless F' = F (for if F' is closer to C than F, then F'C < FC = FE < F'E, contradicting F'C = F'E). Therefore F' = F.

**Step 16.** Therefore F is the centre of the circle ABC, which is what was required to find.

## Proposition 3.2
**Statement:** If on the circumference of a circle two points be taken at random, the straight line joining the points will fall within the circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be a circle, and let A and B be two points taken on its circumference. Join AB [P1]. We must show that the straight line AB falls within the circle.

**Step 2.** Find the centre D of circle ABC [3.1]. Join DA and DB [P1].

**Step 3.** Take any point E on the straight line AB between A and B. Join DE [P1]. It suffices to show that DE is less than DA (a radius), for then E lies within the circle [D1.15].

**Step 4.** Since DA and DB are both radii of circle ABC, we have DA = DB [D1.15]. Therefore triangle DAB is isosceles with DA = DB.

**Step 5.** Since in triangle DAB the sides DA and DB are equal, the base angles are equal, that is, angle DAB = angle DBA [1.5].

**Step 6.** Since E is a point on AB between A and B, the angle DEB is an exterior angle of triangle DAE (for the side AE of triangle DAE is produced to B) [1.16].

**Step 7.** Therefore angle DEB is greater than the interior and opposite angle DAE [1.16]. That is, angle DEB > angle DAE.

**Step 8.** Now angle DAE is the same as angle DAB (since E lies on AB), and angle DAB = angle DBA [Step 5]. Also angle DBA is the same as angle DBE (since E lies on AB). Therefore angle DAE = angle DBE.

**Step 9.** From Steps 7 and 8, angle DEB > angle DBE.

**Step 10.** In triangle DBE, since angle DEB is greater than angle DBE, the side opposite the greater angle is greater than the side opposite the lesser angle [1.19]. Therefore DB > DE.

**Step 11.** But DB equals DA, and DA is a radius of the circle. Therefore DE is less than the radius. Hence the point E lies within the circle [D1.15].

**Step 12.** Since E was taken as an arbitrary point on AB between A and B, every such point lies within the circle. Therefore the straight line AB falls within the circle. Q.E.D.

## Proposition 3.3
**Statement:** If in a circle a straight line through the centre bisect a straight line not through the centre, it also cuts it at right angles; and if it cut it at right angles, it also bisects it.

**Step 1.** Let there be a circle with centre E [found by 3.1], and let CD be a straight line through E, and let AB be a straight line not through the centre. Suppose first that CD bisects AB at F, so that AF equals FB. We must show that CD cuts AB at right angles.

**Step 2.** Join EA and EB [P1]. Since E is the centre of the circle and A, B lie on the circumference, EA equals EB [D1.15].

**Step 3.** In triangles EFA and EFB, AF equals FB [by hypothesis], EA equals EB [Step 2], and EF is common. Therefore by the SSS congruence theorem [1.8], triangle EFA is congruent to triangle EFB, and hence angle EFA equals angle EFB.

**Step 4.** Since the straight line EF standing on the straight line AB makes the adjacent angles EFA and EFB equal to one another, each of the angles EFA and EFB is a right angle [D1.10]. Therefore CD cuts AB at right angles.

**Step 5.** Now suppose conversely that CD cuts AB at right angles at F, so that angle EFA and angle EFB are each right angles. We must show that AF equals FB.

**Step 6.** Join EA and EB [P1]. Since E is the centre and A, B lie on the circumference, EA equals EB [D1.15]. Therefore triangle EAB is isosceles, and by 1.5, angle EAF equals angle EBF.

**Step 7.** In triangles EFA and EFB, angle EAF equals angle EBF [Step 6], angle EFA equals angle EFB [both being right angles, by hypothesis], and EF is common to both triangles. Therefore by 1.26 (AAS), triangle EFA is congruent to triangle EFB, and hence AF equals FB.

**Step 8.** Therefore AF equals FB, that is, CD bisects AB. This completes the proof of both directions: if a straight line through the centre bisects a chord not through the centre, it cuts it at right angles; and if it cuts such a chord at right angles, it bisects it. Q.E.F.
